claim: During development, oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells myelinate central and peripheral nervous system axons, respectively.
source: During development, oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells myelinate central and peripheral nervous system axons, respectively, while motor exit point (MEP) glia are neural tube-derived, peripheral glia that myelinate axonal territory between these populations at MEP transition zones.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about oligodendrocyte and Schwann cell function in myelination.

claim: Motor exit point (MEP) glia are neural tube-derived, peripheral glia that myelinate axonal territory between oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells at MEP transition zones.
source: During development, oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells myelinate central and peripheral nervous system axons, respectively, while motor exit point (MEP) glia are neural tube-derived, peripheral glia that myelinate axonal territory between these populations at MEP transition zones.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' previous work, cited as established knowledge in this manuscript.

claim: MEP glia arise from lateral floor plate precursors.
source: Here, using zebrafish, we found that MEP glia arise from lateral floor plate precursors and require foxd3 to delaminate and exit the spinal cord.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: MEP glia require foxd3 to delaminate and exit the spinal cord.
source: Here, using zebrafish, we found that MEP glia arise from lateral floor plate precursors and require foxd3 to delaminate and exit the spinal cord.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by foxd3 mutant analysis showing MEP glia fail to exit the spinal cord.

claim: MEP glial development depends on axonally derived neuregulin1.
source: Additionally, we show that similar to Schwann cells, MEP glial development depends on axonally derived neuregulin1.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experiments with neuregulin1 mutants and overexpression.

claim: Overexpressing axonal cues is sufficient to generate additional MEP glia in the spinal cord.
source: Finally, our data demonstrate that overexpressing axonal cues is sufficient to generate additional MEP glia in the spinal cord.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by neuregulin1 overexpression experiments.

claim: MEP transition zones are specialized structures where motor axons exit the CNS.
source: Motor exit point (MEP) transition zones (TZ) are specialized structures where motor axons exit the CNS, and where centrally and peripherally derived myelinating glia meet to myelinate the same axons (Fontenas and Kucenas, 2018; Fraher, 1992; Fraher, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: At MEP transition zones, centrally and peripherally derived myelinating glia meet to myelinate the same axons.
source: Motor exit point (MEP) transition zones (TZ) are specialized structures where motor axons exit the CNS, and where centrally and peripherally derived myelinating glia meet to myelinate the same axons (Fontenas and Kucenas, 2018; Fraher, 1992; Fraher, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: MEP TZs were thought to be selectively permeable to only axons.
source: Until recently, TZs were thought to be selectively permeable to only axons, and the establishment of the territories occupied by glial cells remained poorly described and not well understood.
evidence: This describes historical understanding of transition zones.

claim: Recent work demonstrates that MEP TZs are occupied by dynamic glial cells and are precisely regulated over the course of nervous system development.
source: Recent work now demonstrates that MEP TZs are occupied by dynamic glial cells and are precisely regulated over the course of nervous system development (Coulpier et al., 2010; Fontenas et al., 2019; Kucenas et al., 2008b; Kucenas et al., 2009; Smith et al., 2016; Smith et al., 2014; Zhu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to recent literature.

claim: Neural tube precursors generate oligodendrocyte progenitor cells (OPC) that differentiate into OLs and ultimately myelinate axonal segments in the CNS.
source: During nervous system development, neural tube precursors generate oligodendrocyte progenitor cells (OPC) that differentiate into OLs and ultimately myelinate axonal segments in the CNS, while Schwann cells originate from the neural crest and myelinate axons in the PNS (Bergles and Richardson, 2015; Jessen and Mirsky, 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Schwann cells originate from the neural crest and myelinate axons in the PNS.
source: During nervous system development, neural tube precursors generate oligodendrocyte progenitor cells (OPC) that differentiate into OLs and ultimately myelinate axonal segments in the CNS, while Schwann cells originate from the neural crest and myelinate axons in the PNS (Bergles and Richardson, 2015; Jessen and Mirsky, 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: MEP glia originate in the neural tube, exit through the MEP TZ, and eventually reside just outside of the spinal cord along motor nerve root axons.
source: Recently, we described MEP glia, a population of CNS-derived, peripheral glial cells that originate in the neural tube, exit through the MEP TZ, and eventually reside just outside of the spinal cord along motor nerve root axons, occupying territory between Schwann cells in the periphery and OLs in the spinal cord (Smith et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: MEP glia occupy territory between Schwann cells in the periphery and OLs in the spinal cord.
source: Recently, we described MEP glia, a population of CNS-derived, peripheral glial cells that originate in the neural tube, exit through the MEP TZ, and eventually reside just outside of the spinal cord along motor nerve root axons, occupying territory between Schwann cells in the periphery and OLs in the spinal cord (Smith et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: MEP glia express both CNS and PNS identity markers, including olig2 and foxd3.
source: In addition to their central origin and ultimate peripheral fate, one of the unique features of MEP glia is their expression of both CNS and PNS identity markers, including olig2 and foxd3 (Fontenas and Kucenas, 2018; Smith et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: MEP glia express foxd3 before they exit the neural tube, and its expression persists as they migrate into the periphery along motor axons.
source: MEP glia express foxd3 before they exit the neural tube, and its expression persists as they migrate into the periphery along motor axons (Smith et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The function of foxd3 in maintaining the fate of NCCs and repressing melanogenesis is known in chick, Xenopus, zebrafish, and mouse.
source: Although the function of foxd3 in maintaining the fate of NCCs and repressing melanogenesis is known in chick, Xenopus, zebrafish, and mouse, its role in the ventral neural tube where MEP glia originate, remains unknown (Dottori et al., 2001; Kos et al., 2001; Lister et al., 2006; Sasai et al., 2001; Teng et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The role of foxd3 in the ventral neural tube where MEP glia originate remains unknown.
source: Although the function of foxd3 in maintaining the fate of NCCs and repressing melanogenesis is known in chick, Xenopus, zebrafish, and mouse, its role in the ventral neural tube where MEP glia originate, remains unknown (Dottori et al., 2001; Kos et al., 2001; Lister et al., 2006; Sasai et al., 2001; Teng et al., 2008).
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: MEP glia tightly associate with spinal motor root axons and ultimately myelinate the most proximal axonal segments along the nerve.
source: Once in the periphery, MEP glia tightly associate with spinal motor root axons and ultimately myelinate the most proximal axonal segments along the nerve, and therefore, participate in the fast conduction of action potentials from the CNS to the muscle (Fontenas and Kucenas, 2018; Smith et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: MEP glia participate in the fast conduction of action potentials from the CNS to the muscle.
source: Once in the periphery, MEP glia tightly associate with spinal motor root axons and ultimately myelinate the most proximal axonal segments along the nerve, and therefore, participate in the fast conduction of action potentials from the CNS to the muscle (Fontenas and Kucenas, 2018; Smith et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on their myelinating function, supported by citations.

claim: MEP glia function to restrict highly migratory OPCs to the spinal cord.
source: Previously, we showed that MEP glia also function to restrict highly migratory OPCs to the spinal cord (Fontenas et al., 2019; Smith et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: MEP glia originate within the ventral neural tube.
source: MEP glia originate within the ventral neural tube, however, their precise origin and relationship to other CNS cell populations and peripheral Schwann cells, remain unclear (Smith et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The precise origin of MEP glia and their relationship to other CNS cell populations and peripheral Schwann cells remain unclear.
source: MEP glia originate within the ventral neural tube, however, their precise origin and relationship to other CNS cell populations and peripheral Schwann cells, remain unclear (Smith et al., 2014).
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: MEP glia originate from nkx2.2a+/olig2+ radial glial precursors.
source: Using a combination of live imaging, clonal analysis, and genetic approaches in zebrafish, we show that MEP glia originate from nkx2.2a+/olig2+ radial glial precursors and require foxd3 to delaminate from the lateral floor plate and exit the spinal cord via MEP TZs.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: MEP glia require foxd3 to delaminate from the lateral floor plate and exit the spinal cord via MEP TZs.
source: Using a combination of live imaging, clonal analysis, and genetic approaches in zebrafish, we show that MEP glia originate from nkx2.2a+/olig2+ radial glial precursors and require foxd3 to delaminate from the lateral floor plate and exit the spinal cord via MEP TZs.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: MEP glia require axonal cues and classical NCC signaling cascades to migrate out of the spinal cord.
source: We also show that MEP glia require axonal cues and classical NCC signaling cascades to migrate out of the spinal cord.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: MEP glial development is driven by axonal Neuregulin signaling.
source: We demonstrate that similar to Schwann cells, MEP glial development is driven by axonal Neuregulin signaling and that manipulating this signaling is sufficient to generate additional MEP glia from precursors in the post-embryonic spinal cord.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: Manipulating Neuregulin signaling is sufficient to generate additional MEP glia from precursors in the post-embryonic spinal cord.
source: We demonstrate that similar to Schwann cells, MEP glial development is driven by axonal Neuregulin signaling and that manipulating this signaling is sufficient to generate additional MEP glia from precursors in the post-embryonic spinal cord.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: Ventral spinal cord precursors employ NCC developmental mechanisms to generate hybrid, peripheral myelinating glia.
source: Together, our results demonstrate that ventral spinal cord precursors employ NCC developmental mechanisms to generate hybrid, peripheral myelinating glia and bring a better understanding of MEP glial development and spinal motor nerve formation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: All peripheral myelinating glia were previously thought to originate from the neural crest.
source: Although all peripheral myelinating glia were previously thought to originate from the neural crest, we recently described MEP glia, a population of peripheral spinal motor nerve root glia that are derived from olig2+ ventral spinal cord precursors and exit the CNS to myelinate peripheral motor axons (Figure 1A; Smith et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes historical understanding that the study challenges.

claim: MEP glia are derived from olig2+ ventral spinal cord precursors and exit the CNS to myelinate peripheral motor axons.
source: Although all peripheral myelinating glia were previously thought to originate from the neural crest, we recently described MEP glia, a population of peripheral spinal motor nerve root glia that are derived from olig2+ ventral spinal cord precursors and exit the CNS to myelinate peripheral motor axons (Figure 1A; Smith et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and Figure 1A.

claim: MEP glia originate from olig2+ precursors in the spinal cord and exit the CNS through MEP TZs at approximately 48 hr post-fertilization (hpf).
source: In our initial study, we reported that MEP glia originate from olig2+ precursors in the spinal cord and like perineurial glia, exit the CNS through MEP TZs at approximately 48 hr post-fertilization (hpf).
evidence: This is supported by reference to the authors' initial study.

claim: Perineurial glia exit the CNS through MEP TZs at approximately 48 hpf.
source: In our initial study, we reported that MEP glia originate from olig2+ precursors in the spinal cord and like perineurial glia, exit the CNS through MEP TZs at approximately 48 hr post-fertilization (hpf).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: The precise mechanisms that govern MEP glial development remained uninvestigated.
source: However, the precise mechanisms that govern their development remained uninvestigated (Kucenas et al., 2008b; Smith et al., 2014).
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: The vertebrate embryo neural tube is organized according to the expression of region-specific transcription factors along the antero-posterior and dorso-ventral axis in a spatially and temporally controlled manner.
source: The vertebrate embryo neural tube is organized according to the expression of region-specific transcription factors along the antero-posterior and dorso-ventral axis in a spatially and temporally controlled manner.
evidence: This is established knowledge about neural tube organization.

claim: Precursor cells produce different cell types in a stereotypical sequence and the fate of the progeny is determined by when and where they were born.
source: Precursor cells produce different cell types in a stereotypical sequence and the fate of the progeny is determined by when and where they were born (Briscoe et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Distinct olig2-expressing neural precursors in the pMN domain sequentially generate motor neurons and oligodendrocytes.
source: For example, distinct olig2-expressing neural precursors in the pMN domain sequentially generate motor neurons and oligodendrocytes (Fu et al., 2002; Ravanelli and Appel, 2015; Zhou et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Nkx2.2a precursors lie just ventral to the pMN domain.
source: Nkx2.2a precursors, which lie just ventral to the pMN domain, generate interneurons, OLs, and perineurial glia, a subpopulation of centrally-derived peripheral glia that form the perineurium along motor nerves (Briscoe et al., 1999; Clark et al., 2014; Deska-Gauthier et al., 2020; Fu et al., 2002; Kucenas et al., 2008a; Kucenas et al., 2008b; Morris et al., 2017; Schäfer et al., 2007; Soula et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Nkx2.2a precursors generate interneurons, OLs, and perineurial glia.
source: Nkx2.2a precursors, which lie just ventral to the pMN domain, generate interneurons, OLs, and perineurial glia, a subpopulation of centrally-derived peripheral glia that form the perineurium along motor nerves (Briscoe et al., 1999; Clark et al., 2014; Deska-Gauthier et al., 2020; Fu et al., 2002; Kucenas et al., 2008a; Kucenas et al., 2008b; Morris et al., 2017; Schäfer et al., 2007; Soula et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Perineurial glia are a subpopulation of centrally-derived peripheral glia that form the perineurium along motor nerves.
source: Nkx2.2a precursors, which lie just ventral to the pMN domain, generate interneurons, OLs, and perineurial glia, a subpopulation of centrally-derived peripheral glia that form the perineurium along motor nerves (Briscoe et al., 1999; Clark et al., 2014; Deska-Gauthier et al., 2020; Fu et al., 2002; Kucenas et al., 2008a; Kucenas et al., 2008b; Morris et al., 2017; Schäfer et al., 2007; Soula et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: At 48 hpf in nkx2.2a:nls-egfp;foxd3:mcherry embryos, MEP glia express the lateral floor plate marker nkx2.2a.
source: At 48 hpf in nkx2.2a:nls-egfp;foxd3:mcherry embryos, we observed that MEP glia express the lateral floor plate marker nkx2.2a (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), which we and others had not previously observed, while perineurial glia, which also exit the spinal cord at approximately 50 hpf, expressed only nkx2.2a (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B; Kucenas et al., 2008b).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by imaging data in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Perineurial glia express only nkx2.2a at approximately 50 hpf.
source: At 48 hpf in nkx2.2a:nls-egfp;foxd3:mcherry embryos, we observed that MEP glia express the lateral floor plate marker nkx2.2a (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), which we and others had not previously observed, while perineurial glia, which also exit the spinal cord at approximately 50 hpf, expressed only nkx2.2a (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B; Kucenas et al., 2008b).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by imaging data and citation.

claim: Nkx2.2a is a new marker for MEP glia.
source: From these observations, we conclude that nkx2.2a is a new marker for MEP glia.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: MEP glia transiently express olig2 until approximately 55 hpf.
source: Consistent with previous studies, we found that MEP glia transiently expressed olig2 until approximately 55 hpf (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C; Fontenas and Kucenas, 2018; Lee et al., 2020; Smith et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 1C and citations to previous studies.

claim: At 72 hpf in nkx2.2a:nls-egfp;sox10:tagrfp larvae, both nkx2.2a+/sox10+ MEP glia and nkx2.2a+/sox10- perineurial glia are observed along motor nerve axons.
source: At 72 hpf in nkx2.2a:nls-egfp;sox10:tagrfp larvae, we observed both nkx2.2a+/sox10+ MEP glia and nkx2.2a+/sox10- perineurial glia along motor nerve axons (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by imaging data in Figure 1D.

claim: At 4 dpf in nkx2.2a:megfp;sox10:mrfp larvae, nkx2.2a+/sox10+ MEP glial membrane sheaths are reminiscent of myelin internodes.
source: When we looked at 4 dpf in nkx2.2a:megfp;sox10:mrfp larvae, we observed two morphologically distinct cell types, with nkx2.2a+/sox10+ MEP glial membrane sheaths that were reminiscent of myelin internodes (Almeida et al., 2011; Almeida et al., 2018; Fontenas and Kucenas, 2018; Preston et al., 2019), and nkx2.2a+/sox10- loose perineurial cell membranes (Figure 1E; Binari et al., 2013; Kucenas et al., 2008b).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by imaging data in Figure 1E and citations.

claim: At 4 dpf, mbp+ myelin sheaths are formed by foxd3+ cells along motor root axons just outside of the spinal cord.
source: At 4 dpf, we observed mbp+ myelin sheaths formed by foxd3+ cells along motor root axons just outside of the spinal cord (Figure 1F), in a pattern consistent with the location and morphology of MEP glia.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by imaging data in Figure 1F.

claim: MEP glia are foxd3+/sox10+/olig2+/nkx2.2a+/mbp+ neural-tube-derived, peripheral myelinating glia that express a unique combination of central and peripheral markers.
source: By examining various combinations of double transgenic embryos and larvae, we conclude that MEP glia are foxd3+/sox10+/olig2+/nkx2.2a+/mbp+ neural-tube-derived, peripheral myelinating glia that express a unique combination of central and peripheral markers, and identify nkx2.2a as a new marker for MEP glia.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple imaging experiments.

claim: GFP fluorescence in MEP glia dramatically diminished shortly after they exited from the spinal cord in olig2:egfp embryos.
source: In our imaging, we detected olig2 expression in MEP glia. However, GFP fluorescence dramatically diminished shortly after they exited from the spinal cord (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by imaging data in Figure 1C.

claim: At 55 hpf, MEP glial levels of eGFP in olig2:egfp embryos are 4.18 times lower than olig2+ cells of the pMN domain and 7.68 times lower than OPCs.
source: Quantification of the eGFP fluorescence intensity in 55 hpf olig2:egfp embryos showed that MEP glial levels of eGFP were 4.18 times lower than olig2+ cells of the pMN domain and 7.68 times lower than OPCs (Figure 1G,H).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by data in Figure 1G,H.

claim: In situ hybridization with a mRNA probe specific to olig2 did not show olig2+ cell bodies in the PNS near the MEP TZ at 48 or 72 hpf.
source: Additionally, in situ hybridization with a mRNA probe specific to olig2 did not show olig2+ cell bodies in the PNS near the MEP TZ at 48 or 72 hpf (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), demonstrating that MEP glia turn off olig2 before they exit the CNS.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: MEP glia turn off olig2 before they exit the CNS.
source: Additionally, in situ hybridization with a mRNA probe specific to olig2 did not show olig2+ cell bodies in the PNS near the MEP TZ at 48 or 72 hpf (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), demonstrating that MEP glia turn off olig2 before they exit the CNS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from in situ hybridization data.

claim: At 55 hpf in nkx2.2a:nls-egfp embryos, there is no statistically significant difference in eGFP expression between MEP glia, lateral floor plate cells, and OPCs.
source: However, measurements of the eGFP fluorescence intensity in 55 hpf nkx2.2a:nls-egfp embryos revealed no statistically significant difference in expression between MEP glia, lateral floor plate cells, and OPCs (Figure 1G,I).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by data in Figure 1G,I.

claim: Nkx2.2a-driven fluorescence of GFP remained stable after MEP glial exit from the spinal cord.
source: We observed that while nkx2.2a-driven fluorescence of GFP remained stable after MEP glial exit from the spinal cord (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,C), we observed a 2.5 fold-decrease in olig2-driven expression of GFP at these same stages (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,C.

claim: There is a 2.5 fold-decrease in olig2-driven expression of GFP after MEP glial exit from the spinal cord.
source: We observed that while nkx2.2a-driven fluorescence of GFP remained stable after MEP glial exit from the spinal cord (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,C), we observed a 2.5 fold-decrease in olig2-driven expression of GFP at these same stages (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,C.

claim: The olig2 pMN domain and the nkx2.2a lateral floor plate of the neural tube, which are distinct at 24 hpf, lose their defined separation at approximately 30 hpf and merge to give rise to one mixed domain by 48 hpf.
source: We observed that the olig2 pMN domain and the nkx2.2a lateral floor plate of the neural tube, which are distinct at 24 hpf, lose their defined separation at approximately 30 hpf and merge to give rise to one mixed domain by 48 hpf, a phenomenon that has previously been observed and described during OPC specification (Figure 1—figure supplement 3; Kessaris et al., 2001; Kucenas et al., 2008a; Scott et al., 2020; Soula et al., 2001; Tsai et al., 2020; Xiong et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by imaging data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and citations.

claim: At 48 hpf, foxd3+ MEP glia with weak expression of olig2 are observed just ventral to the pMN domain.
source: At 48 hpf, we observed foxd3+ MEP glia with weak expression of olig2, just ventral to the pMN domain (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by imaging data in Figure 2A.

claim: At 48 hpf, floor plate foxd3+/nkx2.2a+ MEP glia are observed.
source: In foxd3:mcherry;nkx2.2a:mcerulean embryos, we observed floor plate foxd3+/nkx2.2a+ MEP glia at 48 hpf (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by imaging data in Figure 2B.

claim: One foxd3+ cell is detected in the ventral spinal cord per hemi-segment of the zebrafish trunk.
source: In all of our imaging, we always detected one foxd3+ cell in the ventral spinal cord per hemi-segment of the zebrafish trunk (Figure 1B, Figure 2A,B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a consistent observation across multiple imaging experiments.

claim: At 48 hpf, olig2+/nkx2.2a+/foxd3+ MEP glia are observed within the mixed olig2/nkx2.2a domain of the spinal cord.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, we observed olig2+/nkx2.2a+/foxd3+ MEP glia within the mixed olig2/nkx2.2a domain of the spinal cord at 48 hpf (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by imaging data in Figure 2C.

claim: The shape and position of MEP glia next to the central canal of the spinal cord are reminiscent of radial glia.
source: We also observed that the shape and the position of these cells next to the central canal of the spinal cord were reminiscent of radial glia (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is an observation based on morphology and position, supported by imaging data.

claim: All ventral spinal cord nkx2.2a+ cells examined are GFAP+.
source: We found that all ventral spinal cord nkx2.2a+ cells that we examined were GFAP+ (Figure 2D; Park and Appel, 2003).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 2D and citation.

claim: MEP glia are generated from lateral floor plate nkx2.2a+/olig2+ radial glial precursors.
source: From these studies, we conclude that MEP glia are generated from lateral floor plate nkx2.2a+/olig2+ radial glial precursors, and maintain expression of both CNS and PNS markers once in the PNS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations.

claim: MEP glia maintain expression of both CNS and PNS markers once in the PNS.
source: From these studies, we conclude that MEP glia are generated from lateral floor plate nkx2.2a+/olig2+ radial glial precursors, and maintain expression of both CNS and PNS markers once in the PNS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations.

claim: Foxd3:mcherry heterozygous larvae label foxd3+ MEP glia as well as neural crest-derived cells, including dorsal root ganglia (DRG) and Schwann cells.
source: While foxd3:mcherry heterozygous larvae label foxd3+ MEP glia as well as neural crest-derived cells, including dorsal root ganglia (DRG) and Schwann cells (Figure 1B–C, Figure 2A–C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and Figure 3A), foxd3:mcherry homozygous larvae, which we will refer to as foxd3-/- larvae, lack these neural crest derivatives as well as MEP glia along spinal motor nerve axons (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by imaging data.

claim: Foxd3-/- larvae lack neural crest derivatives as well as MEP glia along spinal motor nerve axons.
source: While foxd3:mcherry heterozygous larvae label foxd3+ MEP glia as well as neural crest-derived cells, including dorsal root ganglia (DRG) and Schwann cells (Figure 1B–C, Figure 2A–C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and Figure 3A), foxd3:mcherry homozygous larvae, which we will refer to as foxd3-/- larvae, lack these neural crest derivatives as well as MEP glia along spinal motor nerve axons (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by imaging data in Figure 3A.

claim: In foxd3-/- larvae, foxd3+ MEP glia stay in the ventral spinal cord and fail to exit into the periphery.
source: When we time-lapse imaged olig2:egfp;foxd3:mcherry;foxd3+/- and -/- larvae from 48 to 72 hpf, we observed that foxd3+ MEP glia migrated onto peripheral motor nerves in foxd3+/- siblings (Figure 3A and Video 1), while they stayed in the ventral spinal cord and failed to exit into the periphery in mutants (Figure 3A and Video 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by time-lapse imaging data in Figure 3A and Videos 1-2.

claim: Spinal cord OPCs develop at the expected developmental stage in foxd3-/- larvae.
source: Because spinal cord OPCs developed at the expected developmental stage (Figure 3A and Video 2) and the morphology and body length of foxd3-/- larvae were comparable to their control siblings (Figure 3B), we ruled out the possibility that failure of MEP glial exit from the spinal cord was the consequence of developmental delay or perturbed neural tube patterning in foxd3-/- larvae.
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by imaging data in Figure 3A, Video 2, and Figure 3B.

claim: The morphology and body length of foxd3-/- larvae are comparable to their control siblings.
source: Because spinal cord OPCs developed at the expected developmental stage (Figure 3A and Video 2) and the morphology and body length of foxd3-/- larvae were comparable to their control siblings (Figure 3B), we ruled out the possibility that failure of MEP glial exit from the spinal cord was the consequence of developmental delay or perturbed neural tube patterning in foxd3-/- larvae.
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by imaging data in Figure 3B.

claim: By 72 hpf, foxd3+/- siblings have peripheral MEP glia on 100% of their spinal motor nerve roots.
source: By 72 hpf, foxd3+/- siblings had peripheral MEP glia on 100% of their spinal motor nerve roots (Figure 3A,C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by data in Figure 3A,C.

claim: No MEP glia are observed in the PNS of foxd3-/- larvae at 72 hpf.
source: In contrast, we did not observe any MEP glia in the PNS of foxd3-/- larvae (Figure 3A,C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by imaging data in Figure 3A,C.

claim: Ectopic, peripheral OPCs are observed along motor nerves in foxd3-/- larvae.
source: However, we did observe ectopic, peripheral OPCs along motor nerves in foxd3-/- larvae (Figure 3A,D), which is consistent with the absence of peripheral MEP glia (Fontenas et al., 2019; Smith et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by imaging data in Figure 3A,D and citations.

claim: MEP glia are present and can differentiate in the absence of Foxd3.
source: Therefore, we conclude that MEP glia are present and can differentiate in the absence of Foxd3.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from in situ hybridization data showing wif1+ cells in foxd3-/- larvae.

claim: The olig2+/foxd3+ cells observed in the CNS of foxd3-/- larvae are HuC- and therefore not neurons.
source: Analysis of single z-plane confocal images revealed that the olig2+/foxd3+ cells we observed in the CNS of foxd3-/- larvae were HuC-, and therefore, not neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Centrally located MEP glia in foxd3-/- larvae are Sox10+ at 72 hpf.
source: We found that similar to MEP glia in the periphery of control larvae, centrally located MEP glia in foxd3-/- larvae were Sox10+ at 72 hpf (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 3F.

claim: Foxd3 is detected first in 66.66% of MEP glia examined between 44 and 48 hpf.
source: From our data, we observed that foxd3 was detected first in 66.66% of the cells we examined, while sox10 expression was detected first in 8.33% of the cells (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by time-lapse imaging data in Figure 3G.

claim: Sox10 expression was detected first in 8.33% of MEP glia examined between 44 and 48 hpf.
source: From our data, we observed that foxd3 was detected first in 66.66% of the cells we examined, while sox10 expression was detected first in 8.33% of the cells (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by time-lapse imaging data in Figure 3G.

claim: In 25% of MEP glia examined, foxd3 and sox10 were detected simultaneously.
source: In 25% of the cells we analyzed, foxd3 and sox10 were detected simultaneously, likely because we did not detect the cells early enough in their development.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding with an interpretation.

claim: Sox10 expression in MEP glia is subsequent to, but independent of, foxd3 expression.
source: From this data, we conclude that sox10 expression in MEP glia is subsequent to, but independent of, foxd3 expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from time-lapse imaging data.

claim: MEP glia are specified in foxd3-/- larvae.
source: Taken together, we conclude that MEP glia are specified in foxd3-/- larvae.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations.

claim: In foxd3-/- larvae, MEP glia are located in the floor plate at 72 hpf and have a morphology reminiscent of radial glia.
source: We found that while MEP glia were present along peripheral motor axons in heterozygous siblings, they were located in the floor plate in foxd3-/- larvae and had a morphology reminiscent of radial glia (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by imaging data in Figure 3E.

claim: MEP glia do not delaminate from the lateral floor plate in foxd3 mutants.
source: We conclude from these observations that MEP glia do not delaminate from the lateral floor plate in foxd3 mutants.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from imaging observations.

claim: Electroporation experiments in chick show that ectopic overexpression of foxd3 in the neural tube leads to the delamination of supernumerary neural crest like-cells.
source: Electroporation experiments in chick show that ectopic overexpression of foxd3 in the neural tube leads to the delamination of supernumerary neural crest like-cells (Dottori et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: At 55 hpf, supernumerary nkx2.2+/foxd3+ MEP glia-like cells are observed in the CNS of foxd3 mRNA-injected embryos.
source: At 55 hpf, we observed supernumerary nkx2.2+/foxd3+ MEP glia-like cells in the CNS of injected embryos (Figure 3H,I).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by imaging data in Figure 3H,I.

claim: A supernumerary MEP glial-like cell generated in the lateral floor plate of foxd3 mRNA-injected larvae eventually exits the spinal cord at MEP TZs.
source: When we time-lapse imaged these larvae from 50 to 72 hpf, we observed that while a single MEP glial cell exited the control spinal cord (Video 3), a supernumerary MEP glial-like cell generated in the lateral floor plate of foxd3 mRNA-injected larvae eventually exited the spinal cord at MEP TZs (Video 4).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by time-lapse imaging data in Video 4.

claim: MEP glia delaminate from the lateral floor plate of the spinal cord in a foxd3-dependent manner, analogous to neural crest cell foxd3-dependent delamination and migration.
source: From these experiments, we conclude that MEP glia delaminate from the lateral floor plate of the spinal cord in a foxd3-dependent manner, analogous to neural crest cell foxd3-dependent delamination and migration (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data and comparison to neural crest cells.

claim: The boundary between the CNS and PNS is composed of radial glial endfeet that secrete extracellular matrix components to establish a basal lamina.
source: The boundary between the CNS and PNS is composed of radial glial endfeet that secrete extracellular matrix components to establish a basal lamina (Fraher et al., 2007; Lee and Song, 2013; Smith et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Cells secrete enzymes such as matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) to degrade proteins of the extracellular matrix in order to migrate through it.
source: Cells, including neurons and their growth cones, secrete enzymes such as matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) to degrade proteins of the extracellular matrix in order to migrate through it (Hehr et al., 2005; McFarlane, 2003; Yong et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: At 48 hpf, nkx2.2a+/foxd3+ MEP glia delaminate from the lateral floor plate and exit the spinal cord in DMSO-treated control larvae.
source: At 48 hpf, we observed nkx2.2a+/foxd3+ MEP glia delaminate from the lateral floor plate and exit the spinal cord in DMSO-treated control larvae (Figure 4A and Video 5).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by imaging data in Figure 4A and Video 5.

claim: In GM6001-treated larvae, nkx2.2a+/foxd3+ MEP glia delaminate from the lateral floor plate but stall at the edge of the CNS/PNS boundary and rarely exit into the periphery.
source: In contrast, in GM6001-treated larvae, we detected delamination of nkx2.2a+/foxd3+ MEP glia from the lateral floor plate, but they stalled at the edge of the CNS/PNS boundary and rarely exited into the periphery (Figure 4A and Video 6).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by imaging data in Figure 4A and Video 6.

claim: At 55 hpf, 90.61% of MEP glia exit the spinal cord in control larvae, while only 8.58% migrate out of the spinal cord when MMPs are inhibited, and 53.01% are stalled in the CNS.
source: Quantification revealed that while 90.61% MEP glia exited the spinal cord in control larvae by 55 hpf, only 8.58% migrated out of the spinal cord when MMPs were inhibited, and 53.01% were stalled in the CNS (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by data in Figure 4B.

claim: By 72 hpf, 100% of MEP glia are found in the PNS of control larvae, whereas 46.65% are located in the spinal cord of GM6001-treated larvae and only 31.78% are present along spinal motor nerves.
source: By 72 hpf, 100% of MEP glia were found in the PNS of control larvae, whereas 46.65% were located in the spinal cord of GM6001-treated larvae and only 31.78% were present along spinal motor nerves (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by data in Figure 4C.

claim: Foxd3+/nkx2.2a+ MEP glia are observed stalled in the CNS of GM6001-treated larvae at 72 hpf, in a position adjacent to the midline.
source: In contrast, we often observed foxd3+/nkx2.2a+ MEP glia stalled in the CNS of GM6001-treated larvae at 72 hpf, in a position adjacent to the midline (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by imaging data in Figure 4D.

claim: Blocking MMPs inhibits MEP glial migration out of the spinal cord and phenocopies the foxd3 mutant phenotype.
source: From these results, we conclude that blocking MMPs inhibits MEP glial migration out of the spinal cord and phenocopies the foxd3 mutant phenotype.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data.

claim: Mmp17b and adamts3 are expressed in the ventral neural tube at 48 hpf, prior to MEP glial exit.
source: From these studies, we found that mmp17b and adamts3 were expressed in the ventral neural tube at 48 hpf, prior to MEP glial exit (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 4E.

claim: In foxd3-/- embryos, expression of mmp17b is unchanged in the spinal cord at 48 hpf.
source: In foxd3-/- embryos, we observed that while expression of mmp17b was unchanged in the spinal cord, adamts3 expression was significantly reduced in the ventral neural tube at 48 hpf (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 4E.

claim: In foxd3-/- embryos, adamts3 expression is significantly reduced in the ventral neural tube at 48 hpf.
source: In foxd3-/- embryos, we observed that while expression of mmp17b was unchanged in the spinal cord, adamts3 expression was significantly reduced in the ventral neural tube at 48 hpf (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 4E.

claim: No change in adamts3 expression is observed in the spinal cord of embryos overexpressing foxd3.
source: However, we did not observe any change in adamts3 expression in the spinal cord of embryos overexpressing foxd3 (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 4E.

claim: Overexpression of human adamTS3 mRNA does not result in more MEP glial delamination from the precursor domain.
source: Reciprocally, overexpression of human adamTS3 mRNA did not result in more MEP glial delamination from the precursor domain (control: mean ± SEM = 1.06 ± 0.056, n = 18 nerves from five embryos; adamts3 mRNA: mean ± SEM = 1 ± 0.00, n = 29 nerves from nine embryos; p=0.38).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantitative data.

claim: One MEP glial cell per somite is observed stalled inside the spinal cord in foxd3 mutants, just medial to the MEP TZ, in a repetitive pattern along the anterior-posterior axis of the neural tube.
source: In our foxd3 mutant analysis, we always observed the presence of one MEP glial cell per somite, stalled inside the spinal cord, just medial to the MEP TZ, in a repetitive pattern along the anterior-posterior axis of the neural tube (Figure 3A,E and F).
evidence: This is a consistent observation supported by imaging data in Figure 3A,E,F.

claim: Time-lapse movies consistently show one cell exiting the spinal cord at MEP TZs and dividing in the periphery in control embryos.
source: Additionally, our time-lapse movies consistently showed one cell exiting the spinal cord at MEP TZs and dividing in the periphery in control embryos (Video 7).
evidence: This is a consistent observation supported by time-lapse imaging data in Video 7.

claim: Radial glial precursors give rise to a single MEP glial cell progenitor per hemi-segment.
source: This led us to hypothesize that radial glial precursors give rise to a single MEP glial cell progenitor per hemi-segment.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on observations.

claim: 96.67% of MEP glia present along a single motor nerve are the same color in nkx2.2a:cre;ubi:zebrabow larvae at 4 dpf, indicating they originated from the same nkx2.2a+ precursor.
source: When we looked at the color profile of 214 nkx2.2a+/Sox10+ MEP glia along 60 motor nerves at 4 dpf in confocal z-stack images, we found that 96.67% of MEP glia present along a single motor nerve were the same color, and therefore, originated from the same nkx2.2a+ precursor (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by lineage tracing data in Figure 5B.

claim: The color profiles of MEP glia present along the same motor nerve cluster together, while fluorescent profiles of MEP glia present along distinct nerves segregate.
source: Using a ternary plot, we observed that the color profiles of MEP glia that were present along the same motor nerve always clustered together (yellow dots cluster together, pink dots cluster together, and white dots cluster together), while fluorescent profiles of MEP glia present along distinct nerves segregated, indicating that MEP glia along the same nerve share a common progenitor, and that each hemi-segment has a single, unique MEP glial progenitor (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantitative analysis in Figure 5C.

claim: MEP glia along the same nerve share a common progenitor, and each hemi-segment has a single, unique MEP glial progenitor.
source: Using a ternary plot, we observed that the color profiles of MEP glia that were present along the same motor nerve always clustered together (yellow dots cluster together, pink dots cluster together, and white dots cluster together), while fluorescent profiles of MEP glia present along distinct nerves segregated, indicating that MEP glia along the same nerve share a common progenitor, and that each hemi-segment has a single, unique MEP glial progenitor (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from lineage tracing data.

claim: 74% of MEP glia imaged at 72 hpf were EdU+ and therefore proliferated between 50 and 56 hpf.
source: We found that 74% of the MEP glia we imaged at 72 hpf were EdU+ and therefore, proliferated between 50 and 56 hpf.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by EdU incorporation assay data.

claim: 1 to 4 MEP glial cell divisions are observed along motor nerve axons between 48 and 72 hpf.
source: We also quantified MEP glial cell division in our time-lapse movies between 48 and 72 hpf and observed 1 to 4 MEP glial cell divisions along motor nerve axons (Figure 5D), which generated up to six cells per nerve by 4 dpf (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by time-lapse imaging data in Figure 5D.

claim: MEP glia populate motor nerve roots by undergoing cell division.
source: From these studies we conclude that MEP glia populate motor nerve roots by undergoing cell division.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from proliferation assay and time-lapse imaging data.

claim: At 72 hpf, only one MEP glial cell per hemi-segment is observed along motor nerve roots in aphidicolin and HUA-treated larvae.
source: When we imaged larvae at 72 hpf, we detected several MEP glia per motor nerve in DMSO-treated larvae, but only saw one MEP glial cell per hemi-segment along motor nerve roots in aphidicolin and HUA-treated larvae (Figure 5E,F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by imaging data in Figure 5E,F.

claim: CNS precursors give rise to a single MEP glial progenitor cell per hemi-segment in the neural tube, and this cell exits the CNS and acts as a progenitor that further divides to give rise to all MEP glia found on a single motor nerve.
source: This data supports our hypothesis that CNS precursors give rise to a single MEP glial progenitor cell per hemi-segment in the neural tube, and that this cell exits the CNS and acts as a progenitor that further divides to give rise to all MEP glia found on a single motor nerve.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from cell cycle arrest experiments.

claim: Foxd3+/sox2+ MEP glia are detected in the PNS at 52 hpf and as late as 5 dpf.
source: We imaged sox2:egfp;foxd3:mcherry embryos and larvae and detected foxd3+/sox2+ MEP glia in the PNS at 52 hpf (Figure 5G) and as late as 5 dpf (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), revealing that some MEP glia maintain a progenitor state.
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by imaging data in Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Some MEP glia maintain a progenitor state.
source: We imaged sox2:egfp;foxd3:mcherry embryos and larvae and detected foxd3+/sox2+ MEP glia in the PNS at 52 hpf (Figure 5G) and as late as 5 dpf (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), revealing that some MEP glia maintain a progenitor state.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from imaging data showing sox2 expression.

claim: BLBP+/nkx2.2a+/foxd3+ MEP glia are observed along motor nerve root axons at 55 hpf.
source: In these larvae, we observed BLBP+/nkx2.2a+/foxd3+ MEP glia along motor nerve root axons at 55 hpf (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 5H.

claim: MEP glia along the same nerve come from a single progenitor and divide several times to populate spinal motor nerve root axons.
source: Together, these results show that MEP glia along the same nerve come from a single progenitor and divide several times to populate spinal motor nerve root axons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations.

claim: Interactions with axons are essential for Schwann cell migration, development, and function.
source: Because they reside along the same axons as Schwann cells, and because interactions with axons are essential for Schwann cell migration, development, and function (Fontenas et al., 2016; Gilmour et al., 2002; Lyons et al., 2005; Miyamoto et al., 2017; Perlin et al., 2011; Voas et al., 2007), we hypothesized that MEP glial development also depends on axonal cues.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PlexinA3 mutants are characterized by intraspinal motor axon guidance defects that result in ectopic, supernumerary MEP TZs where motor axons ectopically exit into the periphery.
source: PlexinA3 mutants are characterized by intraspinal motor axon guidance defects that result in ectopic, supernumerary MEP TZs where motor axons ectopically exit into the periphery.
evidence: This is established knowledge about plexinA3 mutants.

claim: MEP glia are present along every motor nerve, including ectopic ones, in both plexina3 mutant and WT larvae.
source: We then imaged photoconverted plexina3;nbt:dsred;sox10:eos mutant and WT siblings from 48 to 72 hpf and observed the presence of MEP glia along every motor nerve, including ectopic ones, in both mutant and WT larvae (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by imaging data in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: Motor axons are sufficient to induce MEP glial migration into the periphery.
source: From this data, we conclude that motor axons are sufficient to induce MEP glial migration into the periphery.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from plexinA3 mutant analysis.

claim: In MTZ-treated hb9:yfp-ntr larvae, MEP glia do not exit the spinal cord at MEP TZs where motor nerves are genetically ablated.
source: In these studies, we did not detect any MEP glial migration out of the spinal cord at MEP TZs where motor nerves were genetically ablated (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by imaging data in Figure 6B.

claim: In MTZ-treated hb9:yfp-ntr larvae, OPCs in the spinal cord and Schwann cells along sensory nerves both develop and migrate normally.
source: In these time-lapse movies, OPCs in the spinal cord and Schwann cells along sensory nerves both developed and migrated normally.
evidence: This is a primary observation from time-lapse imaging.

claim: At 72 hpf, wif1+ MEP glia are detected along motor roots in control larvae, but only inside the spinal cord of MTZ-treated hb9:yfp-ntr larvae.
source: At 72 hpf, we detected wif1+ MEP glia along motor roots in control larvae (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A). In contrast, we only observed wif1 expression inside the spinal cord of MTZ-treated hb9:yfp-ntr larvae (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Foxd3+ peripheral MEP glia are observed along motor axons in control larvae at 50 and 72 hpf, but only spinal cord-located foxd3+ MEP glia are observed in MTZ-treated larvae.
source: While we saw foxd3+ peripheral MEP glia along motor axons in control larvae, we only saw spinal cord-located foxd3+ MEP glia in MTZ-treated larvae at both 50 and 72 hpf and did not see any along degenerating motor axons (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by imaging data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Spinal motor axons are necessary and sufficient to drive MEP glial migration into the PNS.
source: We conclude from these experiments that spinal motor axons are necessary and sufficient to drive MEP glial migration into the PNS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from motor neuron ablation and plexinA3 mutant experiments.

claim: Axonally-derived Neuregulin1 type III is essential for many aspects of Schwann cell development, including directed migration, proliferation, and myelination along motor axons.
source: Numerous studies demonstrate that axonally-derived Neuregulin1 type III is essential for many aspects of Schwann cell development, including directed migration, proliferation, and myelination along motor axons (Heermann and Schwab, 2013; Lee et al., 2020; Lyons et al., 2005; Meyer et al., 1997; Miyamoto et al., 2017; Newbern and Birchmeier, 2010; Perlin et al., 2011; Taveggia et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: MEP glia are absent along spinal motor nerves in erbb3b mutants.
source: We previously observed that MEP glia are absent along spinal motor nerves in erbb3b mutants and erbb3b is expressed all along the motor nerve including at motor roots (Langworthy and Appel, 2012; Smith et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Erbb3b is expressed all along the motor nerve including at motor roots.
source: We previously observed that MEP glia are absent along spinal motor nerves in erbb3b mutants and erbb3b is expressed all along the motor nerve including at motor roots (Langworthy and Appel, 2012; Smith et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In nrg1+/+;sox10:eos larvae, red, photoconverted DRG and Schwann cells, and green, non-photoconverted MEP glia are observed along spinal motor nerve root axons.
source: In nrg1+/+;sox10:eos larvae, we observed red, photoconverted DRG and Schwann cells, and green, non-photoconverted MEP glia along spinal motor nerve root axons (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by imaging data in Figure 7A.

claim: In nrg1-/-;sox10:eos larvae, MEP glia and Schwann cells are absent from motor nerve roots at 72 hpf.
source: In contrast, in nrg1-/-;sox10:eos larvae, MEP glia and Schwann cells were absent from motor nerve roots at 72 hpf (Figure 7A), consistent with a recent study showing a reduction in sox10+ cell numbers along motor nerves in nrg1 morpholino-mediated knockdown zebrafish larvae (Lee et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by imaging data in Figure 7A and citation.

claim: Neural-crest-derived DRG are not detected in nrg1 mutants.
source: Consistent with other previous work, we also did not detect the presence of neural-crest-derived DRG in nrg1 mutants (Honjo et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Sox10+ processes projecting through the MEP TZ along motor nerve root axons are observed in nrg1-/-;sox10:eos larvae.
source: We did, however, observe the presence of sox10+ processes projecting through the MEP TZ along motor nerve root axons in nrg1-/-;sox10:eos larvae (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by imaging data in Figure 7A.

claim: In WT larvae, the cell that is the most proximal to the MEP TZ is a MEP glial cell, located in the PNS.
source: By analyzing its morphology, we observed that in WT larvae, the cell that is the most proximal to the MEP TZ is a MEP glial cell, located in the PNS (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by imaging data in Figure 7A.

claim: In nrg1 mutant larvae, the only cell that is present at the MEP TZ is located in the CNS, has the morphology of an OPC, and projects a process through the MEP.
source: In nrg1 mutant larvae, the only cell that is present at the MEP TZ is located in the CNS, has the morphology of an OPC, and projects a process through the MEP (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by imaging data in Figure 7A.

claim: Plp1a is expressed in the white matter of the spinal cord in WT larvae, and also found in the PNS in nrg1-/- larvae.
source: We observed that while plp1a was expressed in the white matter of the spinal cord in WT larvae, it was also found in the PNS in nrg1-/- larvae (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Wif1+ MEP glia are not detected along spinal motor roots in nrg1-/- larvae at 3 dpf.
source: In contrast, we did not detect any wif1+ MEP glia along spinal motor roots in nrg1-/- larvae (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 7B.

claim: Wif1+ cells are found further distally along the motor nerve in the periphery in nrg1-/- larvae.
source: However, we found wif1+ cells further distally along the motor nerve in the periphery (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B), that we never observed in WT siblings and consistent with previous work showing wif1+ cells along the lateral line nerve in nrg1 mutants (Lush and Piotrowski, 2014).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 7B and citation.

claim: In 72 hpf erbb3b larvae, wif1+ cells are not exclusively found along motor root axons as in wild-type larvae, but instead are found more distally in the trunk near the lateral line nerve.
source: In 72 hpf erbb3b larvae, wif1+ cells were not exclusively found along motor root axons as in wild-type larvae (Figure 7C), but instead were found more distally in the trunk near the lateral line nerve (Figure 7C), similar to the nrg1 mutant phenotype (Figure 7B and Lush and Piotrowski, 2014).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 7C and citation.

claim: Nrg1 expressed on motor axons drives MEP glial migration to the motor root, and in its absence, MEP glia exit the spinal cord, but fail to associate with motor root axons and migrate away.
source: Taken together, we conclude that nrg1 expressed on motor axons drives MEP glial migration to the motor root, and in its absence, MEP glia exit the spinal cord, but fail to associate with motor root axons and migrate away.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from nrg1 and erbb3b mutant analysis.

claim: Krox20+ Schwann cells are detected in the white matter of the spinal cord in neuroD:gal4;UAS:hNrg1 embryos.
source: In these embryos, we detected krox20+ Schwann cells in the white matter of the spinal cord (Figure 8—figure supplement 1) as previously described (Perlin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 8—figure supplement 1 and citation.

claim: In neuroD:gal4 control larvae, wif1+ MEP glia are observed exclusively in the periphery along motor root axons at 3 dpf.
source: In neuroD:gal4 control larvae, we observed wif1+ MEP glia exclusively in the periphery along motor root axons (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 8A.

claim: In neuroD:gal4;UAS:hNrg1 larvae, wif1+ MEP glia are detected both in the PNS and in the ventral spinal cord at 3 dpf.
source: In contrast, we detected wif1+ MEP glia both in the PNS and in the ventral spinal cord in neuroD:gal4;UAS:hNrg1 larvae (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 8A.

claim: Several nkx2.2a+/foxd3+ MEP glia are detected in the ventrolateral spinal cord of neuroD:gal4;UAS:hNrg1;nkx2.2a:nls-egfp;foxd3:mcherry larvae at 3 dpf.
source: When we imaged nkx2.2a:nls-egfp;foxd3:mcherry larvae, which label MEP glia more specifically, we detected several nkx2.2a+/foxd3+ MEP glia in the ventrolateral spinal cord of neuroD:gal4;UAS:hNrg1;nkx2.2a:nls-egfp;foxd3:mcherry larvae at 3 dpf (Figure 8B,C), something that we rarely observed in neuroD:gal4;nkx2.2a:nls-egfp;foxd3:mcherry control siblings (Figure 8B,C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by imaging data in Figure 8B,C.

claim: An increase in proliferation of ventral spinal cord PH3+/nkx2.2a+ cells is observed in neuroD:gal4;UAS:hNrg1 larvae compared to their neuroD:gal4 control siblings.
source: Quantification of ventral spinal cord PH3+/nkx2.2a+ cells revealed an increase in proliferation in neuroD:gal4;UAS:hNrg1 larvae compared to their neuroD:gal4 control siblings (Figure 8D,E).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 8D,E.

claim: At 72 hpf, an increase in the number of EdU+/nkx2.2.a+/Sox10+ MEP glia is observed in neuroD:gal4;UAS:hNrg1 larvae.
source: At 72 hpf, we observed an increase in the number of EdU+/nkx2.2.a+/Sox10+ MEP glia (Figure 8—figure supplement 2B), as well as an increase in the total number of MEP glia present along motor nerves (Figure 8—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by EdU incorporation assay data in Figure 8—figure supplement 2B.

claim: An increase in the total number of MEP glia present along motor nerves is observed at 72 hpf in neuroD:gal4;UAS:hNrg1 larvae.
source: At 72 hpf, we observed an increase in the number of EdU+/nkx2.2.a+/Sox10+ MEP glia (Figure 8—figure supplement 2B), as well as an increase in the total number of MEP glia present along motor nerves (Figure 8—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by data in Figure 8—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Nrg1 regulates both MEP glial progenitors and MEP glial proliferation.
source: Together, these results suggest that nrg1 regulates both MEP glial progenitors and MEP glial proliferation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from neuregulin overexpression experiments.

claim: Sox2+/nkx2.2a+ radial glial progenitors are detected in the spinal cord at 4 dpf.
source: At 4 dpf, we detected the presence of Sox2+/nkx2.2a+ radial glial progenitors in WT larvae, which is the latest stage we have assessed (Figure 8F).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 8F.

claim: Nkx2.2a+ radial glial precursors are still present in the spinal cord in post-embryonic development and neuregulin1 can control their proliferation.
source: This suggests that nkx2.2a+ radial glial precursors are still present in the spinal cord in post-embryonic development and neuregulin1 can control their proliferation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation of Sox2+/nkx2.2a+ cells at 4 dpf and neuregulin overexpression experiments.
